s: Athens possesses silver mines of Athens (source of wealth)
q: A mine of treasure in the earth, a fount of silver ore!

s: messenger is a courier (bearing news for Persia)
q: A Persian by his garb and speed, a courier draws anear— He bringeth news, of good or ill, for Persia’s land to hear.

s: Xerxes leaves behind Mardonius (as general with three hundred thousand men)
q: Xerxes went homewards on the way by which he had come, leaving his general Mardonius with three hundred thousand men to strive with the Greeks by land

s: Darius is father of Xerxes
q: Xerxes, son of Darius and of his wife Atossa, daughter of Cyrus, went forth against Hellas, to take vengeance upon those who had defeated his father at Marathon.

s: Atossa is a queen-mother (mother of Xerxes and widow of Darius)
q: See, yonder comes the mother-queen, Light of our eyes, in godlike sheen, The royal mother of the king!

s: Xerxes leads the host
q: Land of the East, thou mournest for the host, Bereft of all thy sons, alas the day! For them whom Xerxes led hath Xerxes lost— Xerxes who wrecked the fleet, and flung our hopes away!

s: Darius is buried honoured burial (a royal heart)
q: There is none like him, none of all That e’er were laid in Persian sepulchres! Borne forth he was to honoured burial, A royal heart! and followed by our tears.

s: Darius controlled the army of the bow (without scathe)
q: How came it that Darius once controlled, And without scathe, the army of the bow, Loved by the folk of Susa, wise and bold?

s: the Persian Empire is a Persian realm (defeated and grieving)
q: O walls and towers of all the Asian realm, O Persian land, O treasure-house of gold! How, by one stroke, down to destruction, down, Hath sunk our pride, and all the flower of war That once was Persia’s, lieth in the dust!

s: the Persian Empire suffers disaster
q: Woe on us, woe! disaster’s mighty sea Hath burst on us and all the Persian realm!

s: Persian army lies low
q: Hark to me, Persians! Persia’s host lies low.

s: Persian army travels to Phocis (and thence to Doris and the Melian gulf)
q: The rest of us our way to Phocis won, And thence to Doris and the Melian gulf, Where with soft stream Spercheus laves the soil.

s: Persian army travels to Magnesia (then)
q: Thence to Magnesia came we, and the land Where Macedonians dwell, and crossed the ford Of Axius, and Bolbe’s reedy fen, And mount Pangaeus, in Edonian land.

s: Persian fleet has full a thousand keels, and ... two hundred more, and seven
q: But—I am witness—Xerxes held command Of full a thousand keels, and, those apart, Two hundred more, and seven, for speed renowned!

s: Persian fleet flees utter disarray
q: No beach nor reef but was with corpses strewn, And every keel of our barbarian host Hurried to flee, in utter disarray.

s: messenger witnesses Salamis naval battle (first-hand witness)
q: As one who saw, by no loose rumour led, Lords, I would tell what doom was dealt to us.

s: Greeks fights for your country’s freedom (sons of Greece)
q: sons of Greece! On, for your country’s freedom! strike to save Wives, children, temples of ancestral gods, Graves of your fathers! now is all at

s: Greek fleet has three hundred galleys at the most, and other ten
q: The Greeks, in sooth, Had but three hundred galleys at the most, And other ten, select and separate.

s: Salamis is strewn with corpses (every beach and each reef)
q: Piled with men dead, yea, miserably slain, Is every beach, each reef of Salamis!

s: Athens is protected by heaven (in ward)
q: In ward of heaven doth Pallas’ city stand.

s: Athens is blamed for Persian defeat (by the Persian chorus)
q: Woe upon this day’s evil fame! Thou, Athens, art our murderess; Alack, full many a Persian dame Is left forlorn and husbandless!

s: Hellas is loved by the gods (as characterized by the Persians)
q: Our myriad hordes with shaft and bow Went from the Eastland, to lay low Hellas, beloved of Heaven!

s: Persian defeat at Salamis destroys hulls (the sea was crowded with wrecks and butchery of men)
q: The hulls rolled over, and the sea was hid, Crowded with wrecks and butchery of men.

s: Persian retreat is caused by Persian defeat (after the naval disaster)
q: His robe he rent, with loud and bitter wail, And to his land-force swiftly gave command And fled, with shame beside him!

s: Darius’s summoning is a funerary invocation (performed for counsel and relief)
q: O Earth, and Hermes, and the king Of Hades, our Darius bring! For if, beyond the prayers we prayed, He knoweth aught of help or aid, He, he alone, in realms below, Can speak the limit of our woe!

s: the gods determine the Fates (as understood by Atossa and the chorus)
q: Yet if the gods send evils, men must bear.

s: the Fates causes Persian defeat (with divine intervention)
q: O queen, our whole disaster thus befell, Through intervention of some fiend or fate— I know not what—that had ill will to us.

s: freedom of Greece motivates Greeks (in battle at Salamis)
q: sons of Greece! On, for your country’s freedom! strike to save Wives, children, temples of ancestral gods, Graves of your fathers! now is all at

s: Persian kingship and power is overthrown Persian defeat (after the loss at Salamis)
q: Yea, men will crouch no more to fallen power And kingship overthrown! the whole land o’er, Men speak the thing they will, and from this hour The folk whom Xerxes ruled obey his word no more.

s: Atossa is adored by the Persian land
q: Queen, by the Persian land adored, By thee be this libation poured, Passing to those who hold command Of dead men in the spirit-land!

s: Atossa is related to Xerxes (mother and royal patron)
q: to my son—if, ere my coming forth, He should draw hitherward—give comfort meet, Escort him to the palace in all state, Lest to these woes he add another woe

s: Xerxes survives the day
q: Xerxes himself survives and sees the day.

s: Xerxes commands all his captains
q: Thy son believed the word and missed the craft Of that Greek foeman, and the spite of Heaven, And straight to all his captains gave this charge

s: Xerxes survives the day
q: Xerxes himself survives and sees the day.

s: Ghost of Darius is a former Persian king
q: was Cyrus’ son, And fifth was Mardus, scandal of his land And ancient lineage. Him Artaphrenes, Hardy of heart, within his palace slew, Aided by loyal plotters, set for this. And I too gained the lot for which I craved, And oftentimes led out a goodly host, Yet never brought disaster such as this Upon the city

s: Xerxes is child of Atossa (son)
q: And thou, O venerable Mother-queen, Beloved of Xerxes, to the palace pass And take therefrom such raiment as befits Thy son, and go to meet him

s: Xerxes builds the ford of Helle’s strait (by artful carpentry)
q: He bridged the ford of Helle’s strait by artful carpentry.

s: Xerxes possesses quiver (nearly emptied)
q: See you this quiver? CHORUS. Say, hath aught survived and ’scaped the fray? XERXES. A store for darts it was, erewhile! CHORUS. Remain but two or three!

s: Chorus of Persian Elders is a aged Persians (truest of the true)
q: Ye aged Persians, truest of the true, Coevals of the youth that once was mine, What troubleth now our city?

s: Persian people is ruled by a lord (peer of the gods)
q: A lord that was peer of the gods, the pride of the bygone day! Then could we show to the skies great hosts and a glorious name, And laws that were stable in might; as towers they guarded our fame!

s: Persian people sinks Persian world (in mighty wreck)
q: Yea verily—in mighty wreck hath sunk the Persian world!

s: Persian army suffers Disaster (through ruin on the deep)
q: Disaster to the army came, through ruin on the deep!

s: Persian army crosses the passage broad (his manifold array)
q: And guide across the passage broad his manifold array!

s: the Persian Empire is in the dust (gone down in blood and bale)
q: The Persian power is in the dust, gone down in blood and bale!

s: Ionians reaps harvest (in the bay)
q: Ionian ships, in fenced array, Have reaped their harvest in the bay, A darkling harvest-field of Fate, A sea, a shore, of doom and hate!

s: Hellas protects Greeks (by exhausting invading armies)
q: By nevermore assailing Grecian lands, Even tho’ our Median force be double theirs— For the land’s self protects its denizens.

s: Hellas causes famine (to invading armies through scarcity)
q: She wastes by famine a too countless foe.

s: bridge over the Hellespont crosses Hellespont (at the strait)
q: He bridged the ford of Helle’s strait by artful carpentry.

s: Ghost of Darius leads Persian army (in many campaigns)
q: And I too gained the lot for which I craved, And oftentimes led out a goodly host, Yet never brought disaster such as this Upon the city.

s: bridge over the Hellespont is built by Xerxes (with carpentry)
q: He bridged the ford of Helle’s strait by artful carpentry.

s: Plataea is on Plataea’s field (corpses transfixed by the Dorian spear)
q: They touch no bottom in the swamp of doom, But round them rises, bubbling up, the ooze! So deep shall lie the gory clotted mass Of corpses by the Dorian spear transfixed Upon Plataea’s field!

s: Zeus punishes hubris (by exacting an account)
q: Doubt not that over-proud and haughty souls Zeus lours in wrath, exacting the account.

s: Poseidon has power Hellespont (cannot be curbed)
q: Ah, folly void of counsel! he deemed that mortal wight Could thwart the will of Heaven itself and curb Poseidon’s might!

s: Ghost of Darius is parent of Xerxes (father)
q: But my son is young And reckless in his youth, and heedeth not The warnings of my mouth.

s: Bactrian force perishes Persian defeat at Salamis (at our side)
q: Ay! old with young, the Bactrian force hath perished at our side!

s: Persian wealth is at risk Persian defeat at Salamis (much I fear)
q: Was it not madness? much I fear lest all my wealth and store Pass from my treasure-house, to be the snatcher’s prize once more!

s: Ghost of Darius is dead death (appears as a ghost)
q: No light thing is it, to come back from death, For, in good sooth, the gods of nether gloom Are quick to seize but late and loth to free!

s: Atossa is a queen (royal mother and consort of Darius)
q: Speak thou, O royal lady who didst couch with me of old!

s: Atossa is spouse of Ghost of Darius (former consort)
q: Speak thou, O royal lady who didst couch with me of old!

s: Atossa is parent of Xerxes (mother)
q: And thou, O venerable Mother-queen, Beloved of Xerxes, to the palace pass And take therefrom such raiment as befits Thy son, and go to meet him

s: Xerxes is young and reckless (in his youth)
q: But my son is young And reckless in his youth, and heedeth not The warnings of my mouth.
